title: Shin
hookLine: the letter on the mezuzah, standing for Shaddai

lines: A SMALL CASE ON THE DOORPOST.
THREE STROKES, JOINED AT THE BASE.
cards: A hallway of apartment doors, and on some, a small case fixed to the right-hand doorpost, often set at a slant. Wood, metal, glass, clay, sometimes a child's art project.

Often there's one letter on it, raised or painted: three upright strokes joined at the bottom, like a crown, or a little flame with three tongues. People pass it every day on the way to work and the grocery store.
Some reach up and touch it as they go. Today's letter is that one.

teach.b: Shin makes a sh sound, three arms rising from one base. The case is a mezuzah, and mezuzah means doorpost. Four steps toward the door.
First, the command. Inside the case is a small parchment, written by hand, with passages from Deuteronomy, including the Shema, whose first word begins with shin. One line gives the case its job.
In the King James words: "And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates." Second, the name.
The shin on the outside is usually explained as standing for Shaddai, a name of God. When God appears to Abram in Genesis, the King James words are "I am the Almighty God," in Hebrew, El Shaddai.

On many mezuzah parchments, Shaddai is also written on the back, facing out. Third, a later reading. Some teachers read the letters of Shaddai as initials for a phrase meaning guardian of the doors of Israel.
That's a reading added later, not the plain meaning of the name, but it shows what people hoped a door could hold.

teach.h: UPON THE POSTS OF THY HOUSE.
teach.b: Some Jews touch the mezuzah going in or out, and some kiss their fingers after.
It takes less than a second, and it turns one of the plainest places in a home into a moment of remembering, right where you cross from private to public and back.
The Shema says to keep these words in your heart, then puts them on the door, where your body passes them whether your heart is ready or not.

how: Jewish homes fix a mezuzah, a case holding a handwritten parchment of the Shema passages, on the right-hand doorpost, often marked with the letter shin for Shaddai; some Jews touch it and kiss their fingers as they pass.

o: the letter for a door, shaped like an open frame
a crown drawn on doors to mark a scholar's home
the three-armed letter on a mezuzah, for Shaddai

games.q: the Shema says to keep these words in your heart. then it says where else to put them. where?
o: on the doorposts of your house, and on your gates.
games.why: on the posts of the house and on the gates. the words go where your body passes them every day.

practice: Picture the door you go through most often, and imagine your hand resting on its frame for a second as you pass. Ask what you carry through it, out into the day or back home at night: worry, hurry, a hard conversation, a good mood.
Choose one thing you'd like to remember each time you cross, and if you pray, let the touch be a small prayer.

wordCard.voice: Shin. The three-armed letter on the mezuzah, usually explained as Shaddai, a name of God, on the doorpost of a Jewish home. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Shaddai, a name of God, as in El Shaddai — the name the shin on a mezuzah stands for.

carryVoice: Your line: shin on the door. A doorway can be a place to remember. I'll be here tomorrow.
